items.issue: The definition says a token is not a byte, but byte-level BPE tokenizers can and do emit single-byte tokens, and a token is often a byte sequence. The same paragraph later allows a token to be a fragment of a character, which is exactly a byte-level fragment.
items.quoted_clause: It is not a word, not a character, and not a byte — it is whatever the model's *tokenizer* decided to carve the text into.
items.fix_instruction: Rewrite chapter-01.md line 9 as: 'It is not necessarily a word, a character, or a byte; it is a vocabulary item — often a byte sequence — chosen by the tokenizer,' so single-byte and multi-byte tokens are allowed.
items.evidence: Quote exact at design/manuscript/chapter-01/chapter-01.md line 9: 'It is not a word, not a character, and not a byte — it is whatever the model's *tokenizer* decided to carve the text into. A single token can be a whole word..., a single character, ..., or in worst cases a fragment of a character.' The same paragraph allows 'a single character' as a token, and for ASCII a character is exactly one byte — so the categorical 'not a byte' contradicts the paragraph's own allowed cases. The chapter also describes byte-level BPE itself (line 15: 'byte-pair encoding (BPE) repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent byte/subword pairs'), whose vocabulary entries are byte sequences that can be a single byte.

items.page_hint: Ch 1 §1, KV cache as a concept
items.issue: The wording says attention is computed 'against the new token.' In decode, the new token's query attends against all cached prior keys/values; it is not attention only against the new token.
items.quoted_clause: so that generating the next token only computes attention against the new token rather than re-deriving the whole prefix.
items.fix_instruction: Rewrite chapter-01.md line 39: '...so that generating the next token computes only the new token's query and attends against the cached K/V, rather than re-deriving the whole prefix.'
items.evidence: Quote exact at chapter-01.md line 39: '...so that generating the next token only computes attention against the new token rather than re-deriving the whole prefix.' In decode the new token's query attends against all cached prior K/V — attention is computed *for/by* the new token *against* the prefix, so 'against the new token' inverts the direction. The manuscript itself states the correct direction elsewhere: chapter-02.md line 27 'The query for a *later* token attends against them [the stored K and V]'.

items.issue: The caption says 'every token' is written one step after it is sampled. Prompt tokens are not sampled; they are processed as input during prefill and their K/V is written then. The rule applies to generated tokens, not all tokens.
items.quoted_clause: every token adds one K/V per layer per head — written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled.
items.fix_instruction: Scope the Fig 1.1 caption (chapter-01.md line 49): 'For generated tokens, the K/V is written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt tokens' K/V is written during prefill.'
items.evidence: Quote exact in the Fig 1.1 caption at chapter-01.md line 49: 'every token adds one K/V per layer per head — written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled.' Prompt tokens are never sampled and their K/V is written during prefill — chapter-02.md line 19: '(a) prefill populates the cache with the prefix K/V and samples the first token'. So the caption's 'one step after it is sampled' rule cannot apply to 'every token'; it holds only for generated tokens.

items.page_hint: Ch 1 §1 'Attention' (final paragraph) vs Ch 3 §3 'Why MoE saves compute but not KV cache memory' (printed page not determinable from chunk)
items.issue: The two chapters give opposite answers to the same question. Ch 1 classifies MLA as 'reduced-width per-token (per-token growth, smaller footprint)' and explicitly separates it from the 'constant-state (no per-token growth)' family. Ch 3 states that compressed latent attention can *stop* the cache from growing. MLA (DeepSeek-V2/V3 style) stores one compressed latent c_KV plus a decoupled RoPE key per token per layer; it reduces bytes/token by roughly an order of magnitude but the cache still grows linearly with sequence length.
items.quoted_clause: Ch 1: "A third family — **compressed per-token KV**: MLA-style latent attention, grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) head sharing — still stores a per-token entry, so its cache *does* grow with token count, but at fewer bytes/token than full MHA."  |  Ch 3: "Only changing the attention mechanism itself (e.g., hybrid/linear attention or compressed latent attention) can stop the cache from growing"
items.fix_instruction: In Ch 3, remove "or compressed latent attention" from the growth-stopping list (leaving hybrid/linear attention), and add that MLA-style latent attention cuts the bytes/token constant (~50-60× for DeepSeek-class geometry) while preserving linear growth; ideally add one canonical three-family taxonomy table in Ch 1 and reference it from Ch 3/Ch 7/Appendix A.
items.evidence: Both quotes found verbatim. Ch 1 (chapter-01.md): "A third family — **compressed per-token KV**: MLA-style latent attention, grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) head sharing — still stores a per-token entry, so its cache *does* grow with token count, but at fewer bytes/token than full MHA. These are distinct mechanisms: constant-state (no per-token growth) versus reduced-width per-token (per-token growth, smaller footprint)." Ch 3 (chapter-03.md @20063): "Only changing the attention mechanism itself (e.g., hybrid/linear attention or compressed latent attention) can stop the cache from growing — KV offload changes where the cache resides, not how fast it grows." Ch 1 places MLA-style latent attention in the per-token-GROWTH family; Ch 3 lists "compressed latent attention" among mechanisms that can STOP growth — a direct contradiction on the same mechanism. MLA stores a per-token latent (plus decoupled RoPE key), so its cache grows linearly with length — Ch 1's taxonomy is the correct one; the finding's byte arithmetic checks: (512+64)×2 = 1,152 B vs 2×128×128×2 = 65,536 B (≈57× smaller constant, linear term unchanged).

items.page_hint: Ch 1 §3 (final paragraph) and Ch 4 §3 'Token Profile in Detail' bullet 3 (printed page not determinable from chunk)
items.issue: The input:output ratio is credited with causing KV-capacity dominance. It does not: KV residency per request is set by the absolute context length (9,200 tokens), not by the ratio. A workload with a 30x ratio and 1,200-token inputs would have ~1/8 the KV per request of the canonical case while keeping the same ratio. The ratio governs the relative prefill-vs-decode *work*; the absolute input length governs KV residency.
items.quoted_clause: Ch 4: "**Input-to-output ratio**: 9,200 ÷ 300 ≈ 30× more input tokens than output tokens. This ratio is [canonical scenario][DERIVED] from the canonical numbers and is the single biggest factor in why this workload is KV‑capacity‑ and prefill‑dominated rather than decode‑throughput‑limited."
items.fix_instruction: In Ch 4 §3, split the claim: the 30× ratio sets the prefill-vs-decode work split; the 9,200-token absolute context sets KV residency and the concurrency ceiling ("KV-capacity-bound because of the long context, not the ratio"). Apply the same split in Ch 1 §3.
items.evidence: Quote found verbatim in design/manuscript/chapter-04/chapter-04.md §3 (Token Profile in Detail): "**Input‑to‑output ratio**: 9,200 ÷ 300 ≈ 30× more input tokens than output tokens. This ratio is [canonical scenario][DERIVED] from the canonical numbers and is the single biggest factor in why this workload is KV‑capacity‑ and prefill‑dominated rather than decode‑throughput‑limited." The claim fails on the physics: KV residency per request = absolute context (9,200 × 2.62 MB = 24.1 GB), not the ratio — the finding's counterexample holds (1,200 in / 40 out is also 30× but 1,200 × 2.62 MB = 3.1 GB, ~8× less KV; 9,200/9,200 at 1× ratio has identical KV). The chapter contradicts its own §3 attribution: §5 Common Mistakes says "long input raises **KV residency**" (attributing KV pressure to absolute length), and Ch 1 §3 frames the ratio as a hypothesis only: "This ratio — input-heavy — is a *hypothesis* that memory (KV cache) and prefill dominate this system's cost rather than decode, not a conclusion token counts alone establish."
